report.summary: Incident S10 was a single 5-minute api-gateway p99 latency spike (1633 ms at 20:00 UTC against a roughly 175-187 ms baseline) that auto-resolved by 20:05 with no customer reports. The system determination is INCONCLUSIVE because the top hypothesis (search-service dependency slowdown, confidence 0.30) is below the 0.50 threshold and contradicting evidence is 50% of weighed evidence against a 35% maximum. Gateway slow-upstream warnings name route /api/v1/search, but the route-to-service mapping is unconfirmed and search-service telemetry was entirely unavailable. No changes were recorded in the 60 minutes before 20:00 UTC, and request rate, error rate, CPU and memory stayed flat. The slow search warnings also occurred at 19:26 and 19:42 with flat p99, and the largest logged upstream time (1079 ms) is below the p99 value, so the logs do not account for the spike magnitude. The root cause therefore cannot be established from the available data.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: An intermittent slowdown on the /api/v1/search path, plausibly served by search-service, produces multi-second upstream responses that inflate gateway p99 for one 5-minute bucket at 20:00. Slow-upstream warnings recur at 19:26, 19:42, 19:59, 20:01 and 20:03, so the search path is a recurring tail source, but the logged maximum of 1079 ms is below the 1633 ms p99, so the logs do not fully account for the spike.
assumptions: The /api/v1/search route is served by search-service, inferred from D02 and the route name only
Logged slow warnings are representative of the tail
The p99 spike shares the same slow upstream calls as the warnings

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: A transient gateway-side stall (GC pause, connection-pool contention or rate-limiter queuing) delays requests for one sample with no visible load or resource change in CPU, memory or request rate. The search warnings would then be non-causal side effects. Pool and limiter metrics were not retrievable, so this cannot be excluded.
assumptions: Sub-5-minute stalls are invisible at 5-minute sample resolution
Gateway-measured upstream durations do not rule out a local stall

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: A brief auth-service slowdown would add latency to every gateway request on the synchronous path, lifting the median as well as the tail. No auth-service latency telemetry was retrieved, and the only slow warnings name the search route, so this is weakly supported.
assumptions: auth-service is on the request path for all routes
Shallow health checks would not reflect a transient slowdown

api-gateway request_rate stayed between 407 and 435 req/s with no step change at 20:00, and error_rate stayed between 0.34% and 0.45% with no change around 20:00.
api-gateway cpu_pct (about 36.5-39.5%) and memory_pct (about 50.5-54.0%) showed no anomaly around 20:00.
Five WARN lines 'upstream response slow' name route /api/v1/search at 19:26:33 (1068 ms), 19:42:27 (885 ms), 19:59:08 (892 ms), 20:01:12 (1072 ms) and 20:03:10 (1079 ms).
Three rate-limiter 'near burst limit' WARN lines occurred at 19:01:25, 19:50:21 and 20:16:01, none within the latency spike bucket.
No ERROR-level log lines were returned for api-gateway in the window.
No changes (deploy, config, feature flag or infra) were recorded for any service from 18:00 to 20:30 UTC; the last api-gateway deploy was v7.4.2 on 2026-09-04.
api-gateway health checks and those of its three direct upstreams (checkout-service, search-service, auth-service) returned healthy at 20:28 UTC, after the blip resolved.

latency_p50_ms and per-route latency series do not exist for api-gateway, so the p50 and route-concentration tests could not be completed.

assumptions: Route /api/v1/search is served by search-service; this is inferred from the route name and the single gateway-to-search edge, not from route configuration.
Logged slow-upstream WARN lines (threshold around 850 ms and above) are representative of the latency tail.

Sub-5-minute stalls would be invisible at the 5-minute metric sample resolution.

(unverified - no valid evidence cited) search-service telemetry was unavailable: metrics returned a retention-gap error and every log query timed out after 3 attempts.

inferred_conclusions.statement: The leading candidate is an intermittent slowdown on the /api/v1/search path served by search-service, but this is not established as the cause.

A transient gateway-side stall (GC pause, connection-pool contention or rate-limiter queuing) remains a viable alternative that cannot be excluded, since no pool or limiter metrics were available and the spike is a single bucket with flat load.
A recent deploy or config change is unlikely to be the trigger, since no change was recorded in the 60 minutes before 20:00 UTC.
Auth-service latency is a weak candidate, since it would affect all routes and no auth-service latency telemetry was retrieved.
Load or resource exhaustion on the gateway is unlikely, since request rate, CPU, memory and error rate stayed flat.
Passing health checks at 20:28 do not rule out a transient fault during 20:00-20:05, because they ran after recovery and are shallow.

remediation.rationale: Observability gaps prevented any conclusion about the dependency and would hamper future incidents.

remediation.action: Add deep health checks or synthetic probes on the /api/v1/search path at a sub-minute interval.
remediation.rationale: Shallow 5-minute-sampled checks cannot detect brief tail-latency events like this one.

remediation.action: Set explicit timeouts and retry budgets for the /api/v1/search upstream if they are not already in place.
remediation.rationale: Bounding upstream slow calls limits the impact of any future search-path slowdown on gateway p99.

brief.title: brief gateway latency blip
brief.alert: ALERT [P3] api-gateway p99 latency 1.6s (threshold 1.5s) for ~4 minutes around 20:00 UTC; auto-resolved at 20:05 UTC. No customer reports.

plan.incident_understanding: A P3 alert reported api-gateway p99 latency of 1.6s against a 1.5s threshold for about 4 minutes around 20:00 UTC on 2026-09-10, auto-resolved at 20:05 UTC, with no customer reports. The breach is marginal and short-lived, so the first question is whether it reflects a real degradation or noise, and if real, what caused it (a change, a downstream dependency slowdown, or a traffic spike). Telemetry covers 19:00 to 20:30 UTC.
candidate_explanations: Transient downstream dependency slowdown (a backend service called by api-gateway had elevated latency or retries around 20:00), propagating to gateway p99
A deployment, config change, or feature flag flip on api-gateway or a close dependency shortly before 20:00 UTC that briefly increased request processing time
Traffic burst or change in request mix (e.g., heavier endpoints or a batch client) raising tail latency without any component fault
Measurement artifact or noise: small sample size in the tail percentile during a low-traffic window, with no real service degradation

findings.summary: api-gateway p99 latency had one 5-minute spike: 1633.34 ms at 2026-09-10T20:00:00Z, against a baseline of about 173-187 ms. The spike is confined to that single bucket and was back to 177 ms by 20:05. Request rate stayed flat (407-435 req/s) and error rate stayed flat (0.34-0.45%). Every WARN in the window is an upstream-slow or rate-limiter warning, and the slow-upstream warnings all name route /api/v1/search. No ERROR-level lines were returned. p50 was not available, so the tail-versus-median question is not answered. The slow-route evidence does not line up cleanly with the p99 bucket and needs follow-up.

observations.statement: api-gateway latency_p99_ms was stable at about 173-187 ms from 19:00 to 19:55 and from 20:05 to 20:30.

api-gateway latency_p99_ms peaked at 1633.34 ms at 2026-09-10T20:00:00Z, the only bucket above about 190 ms in the window. The next bucket, 20:05, was 177.45 ms, so the spike lasted one 5-minute sample, which is consistent with the reported ~4-minute alert.
request_rate stayed between 407.29 and 435.17 req/s over the whole window, with no step change at 20:00. The last value was 407.29 req/s at 20:30.
error_rate stayed between 0.34% and 0.45% (mean 0.40%), with no visible change around 20:00.
cpu_pct (36.5-39.5%) and memory_pct (50.5-54.0%) showed no anomaly, with no change around 20:00.

The window contains 5 'upstream response slow' WARN lines, all with route=/api/v1/search, at 19:26:33 (1068 ms), 19:42:27 (885 ms), 19:59:08 (892 ms), 20:01:12 (1072 ms) and 20:03:10 (1079 ms). No other route or upstream is named in these lines.
Three WARN lines are rate-limiter 'client near burst limit' messages (19:01:25, 19:50:21, 20:16:01). They name client IDs and are not tied to the latency window.
No ERROR-level log lines were returned for api-gateway in the window. All 8 WARN/ERROR lines are WARN.

interpretations.statement: The p99 spike is most likely driven by slow /api/v1/search upstream responses. The two 1.07-1.08 s warnings at 20:01 and 20:03 fall in the spike bucket, and the search route is the only slow route logged.

The slow-upstream warnings are not confined to the p99 spike. Similar slow search warnings appeared at 19:26 (1068 ms) and 19:42 (885 ms) while p99 stayed at about 180 ms, so the warnings alone do not establish the cause of the spike. Logged slow responses may also not be a complete sample of the tail.

Traffic volume and error rate do not explain the spike. Request rate was flat and error rate did not move, so this looks like a latency-only event in the upstream path rather than a load surge or a failure burst.

data_gaps: p50 latency is not exposed for api-gateway. The metrics returned only latency_p99_ms, so the median and its onset cannot be confirmed.
The logs do not name the upstream service behind /api/v1/search, so the upstream cannot be identified from api-gateway logs alone.
The slow-request logs are WARN lines that may be sampled or thresholded (~850 ms+). They cannot show the full set of slow endpoints or per-route tail share.
No per-route latency metric was returned, so it cannot be confirmed whether the p99 tail was concentrated on /api/v1/search.
suggested_followups: Pull the search upstream's latency and error metrics and logs for 19:20-20:10 UTC to see whether its latency spike lines up with the 20:00 p99 bucket.
Query api-gateway for per-route or per-upstream latency metrics, or a p50 series if available, to confirm whether the tail is concentrated on /api/v1/search.
Check whether the 19:26 and 19:42 slow-search warnings were requests with normal end-to-end latency, to explain why p99 stayed flat there.
Check change history for deploys or config changes to the search path or the api-gateway timeout/retry settings near 20:00 UTC.

observations.statement: latency_p99_ms for api-gateway was 184.66 ms at 19:50, 182.18 ms at 19:55, 1633.34 ms at 20:00 (series max), 177.45 ms at 20:05 and 174.72 ms at 20:10.
Three WARN logs show upstream response slow on route=/api/v1/search: 892 ms at 19:59:08Z, 1072 ms at 20:01:12Z and 1079 ms at 20:03:10Z. All are WARN level; no ERROR lines were returned.
One rate-limiter WARN was logged at 19:50:21Z: client a5617224 near burst limit. No rate-limiter WARN appears around 20:00.
api-gateway request_rate stayed between 413 and 431 req/s across the window, with no step change at 20:00.
api-gateway error_rate stayed between 0.39% and 0.44%, with no change at 20:00.
api-gateway cpu_pct (36.6-39.1%) and memory_pct (51.1-53.8%) stayed in normal ranges. Memory peaked at 53.8% at 20:00, a small rise.
The api-gateway metric list contains only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct and request_rate. latency_p50_ms and connections returned no series.

interpretations.statement: The tail is consistent with being concentrated on /api/v1/search, since the only slow-upstream warnings are on that route, but the route-level p99 series needed to confirm this does not exist.

No gateway-side stall is indicated. Pool or limiter saturation is not evidenced: the rate-limiter warning is at 19:50, not 20:00, and CPU, memory and throughput are flat. The slow responses point to the upstream dependency serving /api/v1/search.
Whether p50 moved with p99 cannot be determined. Only p99 is available at gateway level, and the 20:00 spike is a tail-only signal in the available data.

critique.summary: H-A (search-service dependency) is the leading hypothesis but rests on a route-name inference and on warnings that do not line up with the p99 spike. The logged slow upstream responses (max 1079 ms) are below the 1633 ms p99, and the 19:26 and 19:42 slow warnings occurred with p99 flat. issues.detail: Slow search warnings at 19:26:33 (1068 ms) and 19:42:27 (885 ms) occurred while p99 stayed about 175-185 ms. The analysis cites them as support but does not explain why they produce no spike, so they do not establish the 20:00 spike as their cause.

The largest logged upstream response is 1079 ms, below the 1633 ms p99. A p99 of 1.6 s needs slower requests than those logged, or many more slow requests. The logs therefore do not show the magnitude needed to produce the spike, and the claim that the same calls drive the p99 is unsupported.

The link from /api/v1/search to search-service rests only on the route name. The dependency data lists search-service as an upstream but does not map the route to it, and search-service metrics and logs were never retrieved (query timed out, not confirmed unavailable). Confidence 0.40 overstates what is known.
The health check at 20:28 is outside the incident window and is shallow. Citing it as contradicting H-A is weak. Confidence should be lower until search-service data for 19:45-20:15 is in hand.

The gateway-side stall hypothesis is not tested. Per-route or upstream-duration breakdowns and connection-pool metrics were not pulled. Citing the slow upstream warnings as contradicting H-B is questionable, since they are gateway-measured upstream durations and do not exclude a gateway stall.

auth-service is on every request path, so a brief slowdown would lift the median too. p50 was not retrieved, so this cannot be excluded. The slow-route evidence is weak support against it, and no latency telemetry for auth-service was checked.

p50 latency and per-route latency for api-gateway were not available. Without them the tail-versus-median question and route concentration are unresolved. Search-service logs timed out and may succeed with a narrower window and retry.

analysis.response_to_critique: Accepted that H-A confidence of 0.40 was overstated and lowered it to 0.30. Accepted that the 1079 ms maximum is below the 1633 ms p99 and that the route-to-service link is unsupported, and reflected both in assumptions and confidence. Removed the claim that the 20:28 health checks contradict H-A, since they are outside the window and shallow. Accepted that the slow warnings are gateway-measured and do not exclude a gateway stall, so they are no longer treated as contradicting H-B; H-B confidence set to 0.20. Accepted that auth-service would lift p50, which was not retrieved, and lowered H-C to 0.08.

critique.summary: The leading hypothesis H-A (search-service slowdown) rests on gateway warnings naming /api/v1/search, but the route-to-service mapping is unconfirmed, search-service telemetry is unavailable, and the slow warnings recur at 19:26 and 19:42 with flat p99, which contradicts them as the cause of the single 20:00 spike. The 1079 ms maximum is also below the 1633 ms p99. Confidence is overstated given these gaps, and the gateway-side stall alternative is not cleanly excluded. One targeted check of the route-to-upstream mapping and upstream timing could separate the hypotheses with the remaining budget.

issues.detail: Route /api/v1/search is attributed to search-service only by name; no route config or upstream mapping was retrieved, and search-service telemetry failed for every window, so the dependency attribution is unverified.

Identical slow-upstream warnings at 19:26 (1068ms) and 19:42 (885ms) occurred while p99 stayed near 180ms, and the largest logged upstream time (1079ms) is below the 1633ms p99. The slow warnings do not explain the spike magnitude or its single-bucket timing.

The T1 summary says the slow warnings are 'not confined' and 'do not line up', yet the analysis cites them as supporting H-A; the warnings are logged WARN lines with thresholds, so they may not represent the tail sample.

A gateway-side stall remains consistent: CPU, memory and request rate are flat, the spike is one bucket, and no pool or limiter metrics were available. The lack of a sub-5-minute resolution means this cannot be excluded, and the search warnings could be a side effect rather than the cause.
Auth-service is weakly supported; the lack of latency telemetry means it stays low-confidence, but the claim that it would lift median is untested because p50 is not exposed.
Health checks at 20:28 are outside the incident window and cannot rule out a transient fault; this is a data-availability limit rather than something one more tool call can fix for the window itself.

decision.rationale: Stopping with an inconclusive outcome. The leading hypothesis H-A (search-service slowdown) rests on a route name, not a confirmed route-to-upstream mapping, and search-service metrics and logs are unavailable for every window after repeated retries. The T5 dependency task already tried to retrieve route configuration and returned nothing, and api-gateway p50 and per-route latency series do not exist. The 1079 ms maximum logged upstream time is below the 1633 ms p99, and recurring slow warnings at 19:26 and 19:42 with flat p99 weaken the link. The remaining budget (one round, two tool calls) would likely hit the same retention gaps and missing series, so further queries are unlikely to separate H-A from H-B (gateway-side stall) or H-C (auth-service). Confidence stays low: H-A about 0.30, H-B about 0.20, H-C about 0.08, with most probability mass unassigned.
